S1.title: WWW-Authenticate header - HTTP | MDN
S1.excerpt:
A server using HTTP authentication will respond with a `401 Unauthorized` response to a request for a protected resource. This response must include at least one `WWW-Authenticate` header and at least one challenge to indicate what authentication schemes can be used to access the resource and any additional data that each particular scheme needs. [...] A server that supports HOBA authentication might have a `WWW-Authenticate` response header which looks like this:

http

```
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: HOBA max-age="180", challenge="16:MTEyMzEyMzEyMw==1:028: 
```

The to-be-signed blob challenge is made from these parts: `www.example.com` using port 8080, the nonce is `1123123123`, the algorithm for signing is RSA-SHA256, the key identifier is `123`, and finally the challenge is `68147c97-461b-4310-be9b-4c707237ab53`. [...] http

```
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: Digest realm="http-auth@example.org", qop="auth, auth-int", algorithm=SHA-256, nonce="7ypf/xlj9XXwfDPEoM4URrv/xwf94BcCAzFZH4GiTo0v", opaque="FQhe/qaU925kfnzjCev0ciny7QMkPqMAFRtzCUYo5tdS" WWW-Authenticate: Digest realm="http-auth@example.org", qop="auth, auth-int", algorithm=MD5, nonce="7ypf/xlj9XXwfDPEoM4URrv/xwf94BcCAzFZH4GiTo0v", opaque="FQhe/qaU925kfnzjCev0ciny7QMkPqMAFRtzCUYo5tdS" 
```

S11.title: HTTP 401 Error Explained: Causes and How to Fix It | Growthbook
S11.excerpt:
The recommendation here is straightforward: use 401 when and only when the request lacks valid authentication credentials, always include the `WWW-Authenticate` header, and reserve 403 for permission failures. APIs that follow this contract give their consumers — whether human developers or automated agents — the information they need to respond correctly.

## Diagnosing a 401: the distinction that separates a fast fix from a long debug [...] The bottom line: use 401 when the request lacks valid authentication, and use 403 when the authenticated user doesn't have the required permissions. The codes are not interchangeable, and getting this right is the foundation of a predictable API contract.

## Fixing a 401 depends on where in the stack the credential broke down [...] ### What each code tells the client to do next

The distinction isn't just semantic — it has direct implications for how clients should respond.

A 401 response must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header (per RFC 9110), which is an explicit protocol-level instruction: provide valid credentials and try again. This is what makes a 401 a correctable, temporary state. The server is not slamming the door permanently; it's telling the client exactly what it needs to do to proceed.

S12.title: HTTP 401 Error: Meaning, Causes & Fixes | See Steps
S12.excerpt:
## TL;DR

A 401 response code means the server can't confirm who you are: your credentials are missing, invalid, or expired. It's about authentication (identity), not authorization (permission) — that's what separates it from a 403. As a user, you'll usually fix a 401 by checking the URL, re-entering your login, and clearing your cache and cookies. As a developer, check your token's validity, format, scope, and signature, and always return a WWW-Authenticate header. [...] These two codes get mixed up constantly, and getting them straight is the single most useful thing you can learn about the 401 response. Back to our doorman: a 401 means log in and try again. A 403 means stop trying, because reauthenticating won't change the answer. A classic bug is an API that returns a 403 when the Authorization header is missing entirely — that's wrong. [...] A quick note on history, since you'll see older references floating around: the 401 http code was redefined in RFC 9110 (June 2022), which consolidated the earlier RFC 7235. The behavior is identical — if your documentation cites RFC 7235, just know that RFC 9110 is the current standard.

S14.title: WWW-Authenticate - Expert Guide to HTTP headers
S14.excerpt:
A 401 response carries WWW-Authenticate in every case. Responses omitting the header leave browsers with no scheme to satisfy, so no credential prompt appears and the request fails silently. API clients hit the same wall, retrying without knowing which scheme to use. Returning 403 instead communicates a permission problem on valid credentials, which is a different condition. [...] ## Usage

When a client requests a protected resource without valid credentials, the server responds with a 401 status code and includes the WWW-Authenticate header. This header carries one or more authentication challenges, each specifying a scheme and any parameters the client needs to construct valid credentials. [...] After receiving the challenge, the client resubmits the request with an Authorization header containing the credentials formatted according to the selected scheme. The server validates the credentials and returns the requested resource on success.

Multiple challenges in a single response allow the server to offer several schemes simultaneously. The client selects the strongest scheme both sides support. Challenges appear on separate header lines or in a single comma-separated line.

bundles.question: For the HTTP status code 401 Unauthorized, what does it mean according to the HTTP specification, including how it relates to authentication and the meaning of the response in terms of client credentials?
bundles.summary:
- A server that requires HTTP authentication will respond to a request for a protected resource with **`401 Unauthorized`** and must include **at least one `WWW-Authenticate` header** containing a **challenge** that tells the client which authentication scheme(s) are acceptable and what additional data is needed for each scheme. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
- If the client request **already included `Authorization` credentials** and the server returns **`401 Unauthorized`**, then the response indicates that **authorization was refused for those provided credentials** (i.e., they were not accepted for the requested resource). [https://community.postman.com/t/getting-error-401-unauthorized-for-soap-request-after-added-username-and-password/9813]
- `WWW-Authenticate` is the standard mechanism for signaling an authentication challenge to the client in response to a `401`. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
- The `RFC 7235` document defines `401 Unauthorized` in the context of HTTP authentication and `WWW-Authenticate`, but it is explicitly marked as **obsolete** in favor of `RFC 9110`. [https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7235]
gaps: Direct quote/precise wording for the `401 Unauthorized` semantics from RFC 9110 itself (only RFC 7235 and secondary summaries are represented in the provided results).

bundles.question: For the HTTP status code 403 Forbidden, what does it mean according to the HTTP specification, including how it relates to authorization/permissions and what the server is indicating to the client?
bundles.summary:
- **Definition (HTTP spec / RFC 9110, as summarized by sources):** The **403 Forbidden** response indicates that the **server understands the request** and can process it in principle, but **refuses to authorize it**. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403] [https://pulsetic.com/errors/403-forbidden] [https://www.facebook.com/fb-answers/rfc-9110-403-forbidden-definition?locale=ru_RU]

- **Authorization/permissions meaning:** 403 is used for an **authorization/permissions problem**—the client does not have the necessary rights to access the requested resource or perform the requested action, even though the server is not treating it as “not found.” [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403] [https://www.facebook.com/fb-answers/rfc-9110-403-forbidden-definition?locale=ru_RU] [https://pulsetic.com/errors/403-forbidden]

- **What the server is indicating to the client:** The server is effectively signaling: **“I received your request, I understand it, but I will not fulfill it because access is forbidden for your credentials/permissions.”** [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403] [https://pulsetic.com/errors/403-forbidden]

- **Relation to authentication vs authorization:** The sources consistently contrast **authorization refusal (403)** with authentication-style failures (e.g., **401**), emphasizing that **403 is about lacking permission/authorization rather than merely missing/invalid authentication**. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403] [https://pulsetic.com/errors/403-forbidden]
gaps: Direct RFC 9110 wording/section excerpt for 403 Forbidden was not retrieved within the provided sources; the RFC 9110 meaning is only indirectly supported via summaries (e.g., MDN and other secondary pages). [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403]

bundles.question: According to the HTTP specification, when should a server return 401 Unauthorized versus 403 Forbidden (e.g., cases involving missing/invalid authentication vs authenticated-but-lacking permission), and what wording or headers (like WWW-Authenticate) are implied?
bundles.summary:
## 401 Unauthorized vs 403 Forbidden (spec intent)

### 401 Unauthorized — missing or invalid authentication
- A **401** is used when the server **cannot confirm the client’s identity** because the **credentials are missing, invalid, or expired** (i.e., authentication failure rather than an authorization/permission failure). [https://www.growthbook.io/insights/http-error-explained-causes-how-fix] [https://localseomississauga.ca/http-401-response-code-meaning-causes-fix] [https://www.authgear.com/post/http-401-vs-403]
- A **401 response must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header** that provides the **authentication challenge(s)** (scheme + parameters) so the client knows how to form the next `Authorization` header. [https://www.growthbook.io/insights/http-error-explained-causes-how-fix] [https://http.dev/www-authenticate] [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]

### 403 Forbidden — authenticated but insufficient permission
- A **403** is for the case where the server **understands/authenticates who the client is** but the client **does not have the required permissions** (authorization failure). [https://www.growthbook.io/insights/http-error-explained-causes-how-fix] [https://localseomississauga.ca/http-401-response-code-meaning-causes-fix]
- In the distinction described in the gathered material, **403 is not a signal to retry authentication**, because re-authentication would not change the authorization outcome (unlike 401, which provides a challenge). [https://localseomississauga.ca/http-401-response-code-meaning-causes-fix] [https://http.dev/www-authenticate]

## Implied “wording/headers” guidance from the sources
- For **401**, the implied control/wording mechanism is the **`WWW-Authenticate`** header containing the challenge(s). [https://www.growthbook.io/insights/http-error-explained-causes-how-fix] [https://http.dev/www-authenticate] [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
- For **403**, the sources frame it as a **permission problem after valid authentication**, so the client should not expect an authentication challenge in the same way as with 401. [https://www.growthbook.io/insights/http-error-explained-causes-how-fix] [https://localseomississauga.ca/http-401-response-code-meaning-causes-fix]
gaps: The gathered sources describe the 401/403 distinction and `WWW-Authenticate` requirement, but they do not provide the exact normative RFC 9110/RFC 7235 wording or section/paragraph citations needed to satisfy “According to the HTTP specification” verbatim.

No source in the gathered results quotes the RFC text explicitly stating what (if anything) should/should not be included for 403 (e.g., whether `WWW-Authenticate` is prohibited or simply unnecessary) beyond the general behavioral guidance.
